title: Shipping AI to a Million Patients Without an A/B Test — Jared Joselowitz, Ufonia

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

summary: Jared Joselowitz, research engineer at Ufonia, presents the safety and evaluation stack behind Dora, a regulated medical-device voice agent that conducts post-op follow-ups and pre-op checks at scale (~200,000 real clinical calls across 20 UK hospitals, contracted to 1M patients in 2 years). Because randomizing patients into a worse variant is unethical and often illegal, and because a spoken call cannot be rolled back, the standard reactive ship-to-5%-and-roll-back playbook is gone. Ufonia therefore borrows the self-driving approach: simulate before shipping. Matrix uses PatBot, an LLM that plays the patient, validated via a PPI study where real patients often judged the simulated patient more realistic than the real one. BevJudge, an LLM judge, was validated against 10 specialists labeling 240 cases, achieving F1 ~0.96 and near-perfect sensitivity, the metric that dominates because a missed red flag is catastrophic while a false alarm is merely annoying. Hand-tuning prompts does not scale given extreme brittleness (formatting changes have swung benchmarks by 76 points, and reordering few-shots can flip models from random to state-of-the-art). Ufonia instead uses Jeppa (genetic-pareto prompt optimization from the DSPy team), which takes a metric, reflects on failures, and keeps a pareto frontier of best prompts, converging in 30–60 minutes versus hours-to-days. Crucially, the metric is a clinician-defined cost matrix, not flat accuracy: higher reward for catching red flags, lower for missing them, with recompilation enabling different optimized prompts for different objectives. The replacement for the reactive loop is a flywheel: real calls plus synthetic edge cases (rare symptoms, mis-transcriptions) feed prompt optimization, then Matrix as a simulation safety gate, then staged graduation through user testing, supervised clinical evaluation on real patients, and monitored deployment whose autonomy scales with accumulated evidence. Simulation is necessary but not sufficient — it only earns the right to test on real people, who remain the outer loop where real proof lives. Every prompt, judge verdict, and deployment is pinned and traces back to the exact hazard it addresses; what regulators receive is the evidence, not the model. The same framework extends to new modalities such as voice, where new hazards like mid-advice back-channeling and interruptions are enumerated, simulated, and judged rather than discovered in production.

sections.title: Proving a product is safe before a patient hears it
sections.summary: Jared introduces himself as a research engineer at Ufonia working on the safety and evaluation stack behind Dora, a clinical conversational agent. He argues that shipping to patients removes the standard safety nets: you cannot A/B test (randomizing into a worse variant is unethical and often illegal), you cannot undo a spoken call, and a vendor benchmark number is no defense at a post-incident review.

sections.title: What Dora is, and the scale it runs at
sections.summary: Dora is described as a voice AI agent that phones patients for post-op follow-ups and pre-op checks, taking time-consuming work off clinicians' plates. Scale: roughly 200,000 real clinical calls across 20 UK hospitals, contracted to reach 1,000,000 patients in two years, plus a US launch in two clinics with six more signed across four states.

sections.title: A call with a patient after cataract surgery
sections.summary: An audio clip demonstrates Dora conducting a cataract post-op follow-up, asking about blurry vision at distance vs near and advising the patient to avoid swimming for a month. The exchange illustrates that Dora both asks about symptoms and gives advice.

sections.title: Giving advice makes it a regulated medical device
sections.summary: Because Dora asks about symptoms and gives advice, it is classified as a medical device and must be regulated. Regulation boils down to three questions: what does the software do, what could go wrong, and how do you ensure it doesn't.

sections.title: Starting from what could actually harm someone
sections.summary: The team starts from harm rather than from features. Examples include missing a red-flag symptom (sudden vision loss, severe pain), hallucinating an answer to a medical question, and ignoring a distressed patient. There are many documented hazards, sometimes 20-40, and none must occur in real life.

sections.title: Why ship to 5% and roll back breaks here
sections.summary: The standard ship-to-5%-and-roll-back playbook assumes you can afford to be briefly wrong. For patients, 5% means hundreds to thousands of patients receiving unproven changes; calls cannot be rolled back because the harm has already occurred; and a dashboard turning red means a patient was already hurt. The reactive loop is therefore gone.

sections.title: Borrowing the simulation playbook from self driving
sections.summary: Looking to high-reliability industries, self-driving cars did not crash into walls in an RL loop; they drove millions of simulated miles first. Ufonia applies the same idea: Matrix is a simulation framework that recreates real clinical conversations without a real patient, built because you cannot run hazards on real people as a first pass.

sections.title: Matrix, and a model that plays the patient
sections.summary: PatBot is an LLM-conditioned simulated patient used because hired actors do not scale for fast iteration. It is conditioned on a scenario defining exactly what the patient should try to do (for example, asking whether the agent is human or AI), then converses with Dora to produce simulated dialogues grounded in real clinical workflows.

sections.title: Can real patients tell which one is simulated
sections.summary: Validation began with script-adherence checks but then moved to a patient and public involvement (PPI) study. Real patients were shown two side-by-side conversations — one between a real doctor and patient, one between Dora and PatBot — and asked which patient was real. In three of four sets, the majority picked the simulated patient as more realistic, suggesting PatBot is realistic enough for simulation while covering diverse personas.

sections.title: An automated judge, and validating it against clinicians
sections.summary: BevJudge is an LLM judge that scores dialogues against clinician-written expected behaviors and hazardous scenarios, producing structured pass/fail with reasons. It was validated against a 240-case corpus labeled by 10 clinicians from 10 specialties. The top model (Gemini 2.5 Pro at time of writing) achieved F1 of 0.96 and near-perfect sensitivity, matching or beating clinicians — sensitivity chosen over precision because missing a hazard is catastrophic while a false alarm is merely annoying.

sections.title: How brittle prompts really are
sections.summary: Grading thousands of dialogues does not by itself improve the product. The team previously hand-tuned prompts by inspecting failures, but prompt brittleness is extreme: formatting changes alone have swung benchmarks by 76 percentage points, and reordering few-shot examples can flip a model from near 50% to near state-of-the-art. Hand-tuning is subjective, irreproducible, and time-consuming, motivating automated optimization.

sections.title: Optimizing prompts instead of hand tuning them
sections.summary: Jeppa (genetic pareto) from the DSPy team is the prompt optimizer Ufonia uses most. Given a metric, Jeppa passes data through, has a strong LLM reflect on failures and update the prompt, and keeps a pareto frontier of the best prompts until the budget is exhausted. Manual tuning takes hours to days; Jeppa converges in roughly 30–60 minutes and produces a reproducible audit trail, reducing the problem to data quality, feature engineering, and metric definition with clinicians.

sections.title: Making the metric a real cost function
sections.summary: Flat accuracy is not the right metric. Ufonia uses a cost matrix: catching a present red flag is good, missing it is catastrophic, and over-calling an absent red flag is merely annoying. Sensitivity is therefore the primary optimization target, with higher reward for finding red flags and lower reward for missing them. Different clinician objectives (accuracy, etc.) just require recompiling the prompt to produce a different optimized prompt.

sections.title: The flywheel that replaces the reactive loop
sections.summary: The replacement for the reactive ship-watch-rollback loop is a flywheel: real call data plus synthetic edge cases (rare symptoms, mis-transcriptions) feed Jeppa, producing an optimized prompt that is then run through Matrix as a simulation safety gate. Failures trigger relabeling, more data, or re-optimization. After passing, deployment is staged: simulations, user testing, supervised clinical evaluation on real patients, then monitored deployment whose autonomy scales with accumulated evidence.

sections.title: Simulation is necessary, not sufficient
sections.summary: No matter how realistic PatBot is, simulated patients are not real patients. Passing every simulation only proves Dora works in simulation; real-world things will appear that simulation cannot produce. Simulation is the fast, free inner loop that earns the right to test on real people, who remain the outer loop and the only real proof. Clinicians are present at every step.

sections.title: Shipping the evidence, not the model
sections.summary: Beneath every call, dataset, pinned prompt, and judge verdict lies the specific hazard it addresses — that traceability is the real deliverable. Regulators receive the evidence, not the model. Practical takeaways: define your harms, manufacture the rare-but-dangerous cases instead of waiting, make the evaluation metric a real cost function, and pin prompt versions with full traces. The work is never done; new modalities and languages bring new hazards, but the same framework applies.

sections.title: New modalities bring new hazards, same framework
sections.summary: Voice introduces hazards that text does not, notably back-channeling and interruptions: a weak model giving safety advice (e.g. 'you must avoid bright lights') can be cut off by a patient and simply drop the advice to answer the next question. The framework does not change — the system is still black-boxed, new hazards are written down, and Matrix simulates and judges them. Voice is just a new module in the same safety case, and Matrix is used in the voice space exactly as in text.
